extracted.intended_audience: teachers (district/elementary school teachers) seeking classroom management and moral-instruction methods
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for securing order, moral instruction, and cooperative conduct in elementary/district school classrooms using persuasion, example, and carefully timed public influence rather than merely authoritative punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure a majority by gentle measures
rubrics_metrics.description: To interest and gain over to our side, the majority — use mild, persuasive measures to secure a cooperating majority of scholars rather than relying solely on authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's stated object is 'to interest and gain over to our side, the majority.' Expect to win the majority by appealing to pupils' tastes and by engaging them in the school's life; this narrows the field of discipline and makes it easier to handle the few who remain refractory. Do not assume majority behavior will happen without active cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and study pupils before acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Before attempting to correct disorder, the teacher should 'simply observes' — watch for faults without haste, study the materials (pupils) and let their true character develop before intervening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch 'without seeming to watch' during exercises, try to find something to approve in the exercise, and use that as a lever for interest. Avoid immediate 'artillery of reproof' and threats; premature harshness gains mere external compliance. Time your interventions after you have learned who can be influenced by mild measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interest, narratives and analogies to motivate reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest the class in reform by narrating facts or making explanations connected with the exercise (e.g., comparing the class to strict vs. lax military companies) rather than commanding by force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: using the image of a strict military company to produce an involuntary straightening of posture and voluntary formation of a line. Employ stories and analogies that evoke pride in order to produce willing cooperation instead of coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer private handling of unpleasant disciplinary matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend to everything unpleasant in the discipline of the school, as far as possible, privately; public punishments should be rare and deliberate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public reproofs often harden the school and produce unpleasant associations; they punish the bystanders as much or more than the offender. If a case must be noticed publicly, state that it received attention but carry out the ultimate disposal privately. Avoid making the school's last impression of the day one of suffering and terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only bring cases publicly when public opinion will support it
rubrics_metrics.description: Never bring forward a case of discipline publicly unless you are sure that public opinion will go in your favor; otherwise publicizing the case may do more harm than good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the school's sympathy is stirred for the 'criminal' in a way that turns opinion against the teacher, public exposure will backfire. Choose timing and form so that the public effect benefits the school's moral tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use occasional public examples strategically for general moral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a particular case arises that can be used to influence the whole school, bring it forward in a public manner only for its general effect and arrange what is said and done to maximize the public moral impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: the teacher rescues a mischief-maker from a mob but later retells the rescue anonymously to turn the school's opinion against the boy's ingratitude, thereby stopping malicious tricks. Such opportunities are rare but powerful; teachers should constantly watch for such emergencies and plan to use them to shape public sentiment rather than merely punish the individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate strictness of measures from gentleness of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the measures you take to prevent wrong strict, authoritative, and uniform, but keep your feelings of displeasure mild and gentle in manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform, systematic measures do not offend when applied calmly, whereas a morose look, harsh expression, or fretful tone is deeply unpopular and counterproductive. Be decisive in actions but moderate in personal demeanor; avoid scolding as a substitute for effective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scolding; general instruction rather than general reproof
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression of displeasure (scolding) will seldom or never do any good — it operates simply as punishment and produces unpleasantness without moral improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve reproof for cases where it serves a defined purpose; give general instruction on duty but avoid frequent rebukes. Scolding tires pupils and erodes good humor and receptivity to moral teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model the rules and submit to the same restraints you require
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should feel and show they are under obligation as well as the scholars and extend the school's authority over themselves; submit to rules you expect of pupils unless a different course is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: if a study card marks recess time, the teacher should stop speaking instantly when the bell rings, demonstrating obedience to the system. Such modeling teaches fidelity and obedience more effectively than scolding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead pupils to share credit and responsibility for the school
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead pupils to see that they share with the teacher the credit or disgrace that success or failure brings, cultivating an attachment to the institution and interest in its public reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely tell pupils they are responsible; speak about the school's reputation and repeat judiciously what is said for and against the school to make them feel invested. Where rivalry exists with other schools, guide the feeling so it produces diligence rather than mere external defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give moral instruction via general/imaginary cases and pupil-written exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: When teaching moral duty, take up the subject generally (imaginary or unknown cases) and use student-written short papers as the basis for reading and comment to excite interest and deepen effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: assign a moral subject, distribute small papers, ask pupils to write their thoughts in a short time, then read and comment. Examples include topics like 'Prejudice,' with teacher comments and discussion following. This method engages pupils' minds and avoids the impression that instruction is merely to remove a teacher's inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct prejudices by associating pleasant ideas with the object
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudices are usually founded on unpleasant associations; to remove them, connect pleasant associations with the object of prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: soften antipathy to spiders by showing their interesting behavior (web-building, care of eggs) to create pleasant curiosity. For social prejudices, encourage experiences and associations that counteract the unpleasant ones. The remedy is associative and experiential rather than merely didactic.
